title: Navy won’t rename carrier slated to honor Black war hero after considering switching it to Trump | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The US Navy is no longer considering renaming an aircraft carrier under construction that was set to honor a Black sailor hailed for his heroic actions during the attack on Pearl Harbor.

During President Donald Trump’s first term, the Navy announced that the Ford-class carrier would be called the USS Doris Miller, recognizing an enlisted sailor who helped defend US forces from Japan’s attack.

CNN reported in August that there were internal conversations aboutrenamingthe carrier to honor Trump, according to two sources familiar with the discussions. When asked in August, the Navy had no comment and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to announce at that time.

In a statement Friday to CNN, a spokesperson for Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said, “There is no intention to change the name of the USS Doris Miller.”

The choice to name the ship after Miller marked the first time an aircraft carrier would honor an enlisted sailor, and the first aircraft carrier to be named for an African American.

Miller’s great-nephew, Thomas Bledsoe, applauded the news as a historic moment for his family that will preserve Miller’s legacy of “courage, sacrifice, and service to our nation.”

“Doris Miller’s story is not just our family’s history; it is American history. His courage deserves to be remembered, honored, and recognized for generations to come,” Bledsoe said.

CNN reported in August that the Navy was recommending Miller for the Medal of Honor, the highest decoration for military valor. The final authorization for the award is up to Congress and approval from Trump.

Doris “Dorie” Miller, from Waco, Texas, enlisted in the US Navy in 1939, according to the National Museum of the Pacific War. On the day of Japan’s attack, Miller — a Mess Attendant Third Class at the time — was retrieving laundry when bombs began falling on the US fleet. Mess attendant was one of the only jobs in the Navy open to Black men, according to the Department of Veteran Affairs. Damage by Japan’s attack kept him from returning to his assigned battle station.

Miller proceeded to aid his wounded commanding officer, and then, despite having received no training on the system, took control of an anti-aircraft gun and opened fire on the Japanese aircraft.

“Although untrained,” the VA’s website says, “he laid down effective fire and stopped firing when he ran out of ammunition and the ship began to sink. Even then, he persisted in helping his fellow sailors to safety until he finally made his way to shore.”

Miller was famously portrayed by Cuba Gooding Jr. in the 2001 film “Pearl Harbor.”

In 1942, Admiral Chester Nimitz presented Miller with the Navy Cross, and he was then sent out on a War Bond tour with several white service members, “making him the first African American allowed on the speaking tour,” according to the VA. Roughly a year later, Miller was killed during the Battle of Makin when his ship was hit by a Japanese submarine’s torpedo.

CNN’s Haley Britzky and Pamela Brown contributed to this report.
